# **Monthly precious metal report** 

_Gold, silver, platinum and palladium February 2012_ 

**David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** 

**19 March 2012** 

#### **New York:** 

- Although the prices of many of the precious metals climbed during February, the market taught some less wary investors a valuable and expensive lesson as prices crashed on the last day of the month. While prices had been rising solidly for the first two months of 2012 and the last few months of 2011 too, risk seems to be underpriced with the market remarkably relaxed about the prospects of default and disorder in the European financial markets. 

• For the platinum group metals, some of the price strength seemed reasonable as the Impala strike proved more difficult to resolve than many had previously thought, leading to losses of platinum, palladium and rhodium production. However, in our view, the price premium in each of these metals which could be attributed to this supply side disruption was actually rather small. Instead, we believe that the majority of the price strength was generated by a widespread scramble for assets similar to what happened in the lead-up to QE2. 

• During February, we visited a range of Asian markets to gain a birds-eye view of investor behaviour and of real physical demand. Asian buying interest of gold continues to be strong but is composed of an ill-fitting combination of collateralised deals, physical investment and strong jewellery demand. Silver demand seems much weaker, with physical end-user buying much less strong than was the case last year, although it may be starting to improve. Palladium demand from industrial and automotive users seems to be robust - even if Chinese economic growth is slower than might be desired, it is still growth - while platinum uptake by industrial consumers looks set to be weaker than in 2011.

rch 2012** ## **Overview** Precious metal prices performed strongly during February if the last day of the month is excluded, with all of the major metals rising in price terms and even rhodium and ruthenium gaining ground too . We tend to view investor activity as less important in the minor platinum group metal market than in the four major metals and the fact that all of the metals increased in value could be taken to indicate that demand was particularly strong across the complex. However, this was certainly not universally the case: while demand is good for some metals, for others, such as silver in particular, it seems rather weak. There were plenty of indications of decent real gold demand from the world’s central banks and from the jewellery sector during a successful Chinese New Year. The changes to import duties in India seem to have had little real negative impact and demand was at least consistent although Japanese physical demand for gold was a little slower than had been the case right at the start of the year. All of this provided support for higher prices as did a measured degree of ETF buying of the yellow metal and a more carefree throw of the dice by futures speculators looking to take longer and longer positions. **_Figure 1_** _: We believe the Dollar weakness of January and February is unlikely to persist throughout the rest of H1 2012._ A strengthening Euro also helped drive higher prices throughout the precious metals complex. It is a reasonable question to ask why the Euro strengthened but despite its many problems, with almost everyone in the financial markets now expecting a Greek default (or a carefully-worded legal interpretation of a default) to take place, there was no real need for investors to build even more bearish positions on the Euro. Nonetheless, we feel that there may be other unpleasant surprises lurking in the European woodshed, and that this Euro strength is likely to be short-lived and transitory. In platinum and palladium, price support appears to have come from the investor community too, both in the futures market where interest was revived to a surprising extent and in the Exchange Traded Funds where last year’s selling in both metals was replaced by new buying almost as the clocks chimed midnight on New Year’s Eve. Demand was not really the most important story, though, supply seemed to be more important. In particular, the continuing disruption at the Impala Lease Area (which now appears to be largely resolved) provided some support. Although this was painted as a platinum story with figures of 20,000 ounces of platinum lost per week of the illegal strike, we feel that it provided as much support for palladium, a tighter market where more than 10,000 ounces of metal should also have been lost per we

ek. 

Altogether, there were enough positive influences for all of the metals to climb throughout February. Gold rose from $1,744 at the start of the month to a final fix of $1,770 on the 29th before plummeting while silver firmed from $33.80 to $37.23 before falling back on the final day of the month. Platinum and palladium gained 7.1 and 4.2 per cent respectively from their opening $1,611 and $693. 



3 

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 March 2012** 

However, the influence of speculators and other investors was certainly visible at the end of the month of February. Once the European Central Bank (ECB) had released data for the latest round of borrowing by commercial banks (the so-called LTRO) to little impact, Ben Bernanke came to the fore, making his usual biannual testimony to Congress. 

After the fact, some commentators noted that his comments may have further played down the likelihood of US quantitative easing but that seems unlikely to have been the real reason for the blood-letting that followed (although some of the wilder conspiracy theories seem even less likely to have been the cause). Whatever the real reason, the Dollar rose sharply and the precious metals plunged along with oil. Gold fell almost $100 and silver almost $3 in a very short period. The platinum group metals were not immune and fell too but seemed rather more resilient. Gold ended the month at $1,697, silver at $35.11 and platinum and palladium at $1,693 and $707 respectively. Although all four metals gained in price terms during the month, the final taste they left with many investors was sour and investor behaviour has been much more measured in early March. 

### **Iran, Israel and oil** 

As we stated at the start of the year, it is almost impossible to forecast which issues will become particularly important in the global economy over the coming twelve months. The Greek debt crisis was one notable exception for this year but the impact of growing Iranian/Israeli political tension is a good example of a market surprise which has intensified more quickly than we had expected. 

Although many newspapers will give a more nuanced and informed view of the situation, the widespread belief is a) that Iran is trying to develop nuclear weapons, b) that it will soon move parts of this development process underground, making it harder to disrupt in the future and c) that Israel may launch a conventional attack on some Iranian facilities before this happens. The outlook is complicated by the fact that this is a US presidential election year and that Middle East politics are seemingly of great relevance in internal US politics. 

Whatever the rights and wrongs and realities of the situation are, it is clearly having an impact on world energy markets. A European embargo on buying Iranian oil is being gradually enacted and US sanctions against trading with Iran are already in place. Although this oil will probably simply be sold to othe

r customers, the prospect of reduced sales by Iran and possible disruption to shipping through the strategically-important Straits of Hormuz have placed upside pressure on oil prices: Brent crude has risen from $107 per barrel at the start of the year to $123 at the start of March, an increase of 14.2 per cent. But how does this affect the rest of the world economy and the precious metals markets in particular, assuming that no conflict actually breaks out? The principal effects stem directly from the rise in the oil price. Firstly, this could start to slow the global economic recovery and even place further downwards pressure on underperforming regions. This should be negative for the prices of commodities where demand is intimately linked to economic demand. Gold could therefore fare better than silver and the platinum group metals in price terms if oil prices continue to rise rapidly and impinge upon economic output. A high oil price will also lead to higher inflation in almost every country as energy prices rise. This is particularly true in developing countries where energy is a larger proportion of the populace’s normal daily costs and therefore more important in inflation terms. For countries such as India, Indonesia and Malaysia, where widespread fuel subsidies exist, there will also be pressure on government budgets. Generally, oil’s contribution to inflation will give many governments less room to manoeuvre in reducing interest rates, meaning that they may struggle to weaken their currencies and prevent them appreciating. One potential impact of this is slower economic growth in these economies and therefore 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 March 2012** weaker industrial demand for commodities. The final question is whether the precious metals, and gold in particular, can recapture their relationship to geopolitical risk. Prior to 2007 and the global economic crisis, escalating Middle East tensions were typically positive for oil prices and also positive for gold. The natural link between gold and the other metals would often also mean that sabrerattling was positive for the prices of the other metals too. We feel that the link between gold and oil in these situations has weakened but, as is shown in the graph below, there are indications that they could be strengthening once again. Thus, while these sorts of political developments are unwelcome, they could be positive for at least some precious metal prices. Price correlations with oil

### **Gold as a safe haven** 

After the sharp fall in the gold price at the end of Q3 2011 and again after the rollercoaster ride (or perhaps bungee jump) at the end of February 2012, we have seen widespread comments questioning whether gold or the other precious metals deserve to be accorded safe haven status. Can an asset which loses more than five per cent of its value in a single day be termed a safe haven from risk? 

Well, perhaps yes. A sane person buying a safe haven would generally like to dodge much of the volatility prevalent in current asset markets. However, should one really mark a safe haven asset to market on a daily basis? The haven is not against all price movements but surely against longer term price trends? To this end, even a $100 daily fall is not a reason against holding this metal. Likewise, a safe haven should not be purchased on the spur of the moment, it is meant to be bought slowly, over time. So, a $100 spike in the price should not be a reason not to buy and a $100 fall should only be a gentle reminder that buying might be sensible at some point. It is also reasonable to ask whether an insurance policy should be expected to pay out when only limited damage has been done to the capital at risk. Viewed in this light, it is possible and reasonable to be more positive about gold’s potential role as a financial asset. 

Much of gold’s safe haven role depends on how the metal is purchased. For futures investors using leveraged positions, gold is not a particularly safe asset if prices can move as far and as fast as they did on the 29<sup>th</sup> of February. However, for physical investors who are more interested in gold’s longer term benefits, gold still looks like a reasonable asset to known as insurance. From a practical viewpoint, any Dollar-based investor who bought

**19 March 2012** 

gold at _any_ point in the last twelve years prior to August 2011 has made money and avoided losses in some very challenging equity markets. For a Chinese investor, the Shanghai Stock Exchange composite index is still little more than a third of its peak value. By comparison, gold seems to have been a very safe haven indeed. 

Of more concern is the correlation between the gold price and the price of other competitive assets (typically including equities). To be a true safe haven, gold needs either to stand passively as equity markets fall or to gain in value at that time. In Dollar terms, there is no doubt it has failed this test in recent months. The simple risk-on, risk-off investment dynamic has been problematic for gold investors. Where gold might normally have benefited from a risk premium, it has often been sold off on risk events and this certainly tarnishes gold’s allure to Western

investors. 

However, we remain believers in the relevance of physical demand and of Asian consumers to the gold market. For these “investors” gold is not a diversification from equities but rather from commodities and it is diversified by virtue of its fungibility, its liquidity and the international nature of its price discovery. For these consumers and others, we believe that gold remains, albeit imperfectly, a rather attractive hedge against almost any economic disaster that can be imagined.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 March 2012** 

## **<mark>Gold</mark>** 

One current conundrum in the gold market is how investors maintain their near-universal belief in higher prices given that the yellow metal has traded sideways or worse since August in Dollar terms. In the context of the more than ten year bull run in Dollar gold, this period of soft performance stands out starkly. Yet, relatively few commentators or investors have taken this as a cue to become bearish of gold prices. 

**_Figure 3_** _: Is the gold price trending higher or lower in US Dollar terms?_ 



The market consensus over the gold price is mixed in the medium term. However, in the shorter term, most commentators expect gold to challenge its nominal highs of $1,900 or so at some point during the current calendar year. For a range of reasons, we also tend to argue for higher gold prices both in the short and in the medium term. However, we also accept the occasional spell of illogical behaviour and the existence of feedback mechanisms within the metal price. 

So, to us, the move higher in January and February seemed entirely logical and reasonable. Gold started the year at $1,566 and climbed to end January at $1,737 with considerable help from a Euro that showed more resilience than anyone had really expected. February was much less more positive for gold bugs: a sudden dose of reality in the foreign exchange markets prevented gold moving too much higher despite a general rush to firmer prices for a range of assets. This was despite the continuing saga of the Greek bailout where sentiment worsened as European governments considered providing only half a bailout unless they were given further assurances over yet more Greek austerity. Although Europeans continue to be healthy buyers of gold, it seems that yet more fresh stimuli may be required to drive gold prices higher still. 

Gold peaked at $1,784 on the 28th of February as some gentle ETF buying provided light encouragement to investors. However, even this peak was lower than the high made in November which was itself lower than the nominal record prices of August 2011, a worrying trend. Right at the end of the month came the most vicious price action. The market focused most of its attention on the release of information on uptake of the ECB’s latest long term credit facility. This seemed to have little impact on the market. More important was Ben Bernanke’s latest testimo

ny to the US legislature. This seemed to indicate a lower likelihood of QE3 than investors had previously thought, triggering a sell-off of a range of assets. This did not, though, appear to be the whole story, violent selling came into the market and gold plummeted $100 in quick order before finding some support. As a result, the gold price ended the month at $1,697, $40 below from where it had started February.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 March 2012** 

### **Gold investment** 

Physical gold demand appeared to remain strong during February, although there were some indications of a slight softness in Chinese demand following the Chinese New Year. ETF flows were positive throughout as they has been in January. However, they were unimpressive in scale considering the unconvincing nature of progress over the Greek debt situation. Nonetheless, ETF holdings climbed above 70 million ounces of gold (in the funds which we monitor, which includes all of the largest ETFs) to their highest level since their original launch back in 2003. At current levels of interest, we do not feel that ETF buying is strong enough to prompt a move to higher bullion prices. 

**_Figure 4_** _: ETF flows are supportive of the price but are unlikely to drive it back to record levels on their own._ 



However, the picture is quite different with respect to the futures and options markets. With most investors positive about the outlook for almost anything that they could buy, net long speculative positions on COMEX climbed sharply, rising from a low of 16.8 million ounces at the start of the year to 27.6 million ounces on the 28th of February. The simple addition to long positions held by investors was fairly impressive but was a little underwhelming on two fronts. Firstly, net positions still remained some reasonable distance below their peak level of 2011, suggesting that not everyone was convinced of the bullish case for gold. We monitor rolling “flows” of COMEX positions and, although a large number of fresh long positions were added by investors, the scale of these flows was lower than has been the case in recent months. More worryingly still, the speed of these flows has now been slowing for almost three years, as can be seen in the chart below. As with the ETF flows discussed above, the scale of buying seems to be weakening gradually over time and we feel that fresh stimuli may be needed to drive futures positions back to record levels and help prices higher. 



**_Figure 5_** _:  A price graph like this would clearly be trending lower. Should we likewise believe that the intensity of futures buying is slipping lower too?_

### **Chinese physical demand** 

We believe that the best way to monitor gold demand within China is by using proxy data from Shanghai Gold Exchange trading. Straight year-on-year comparisons are

meaningless at the start of the year since the lunar Chinese New Year (CNY) moves date. However, this is a key buying season for the jewellery industry. We therefore look at sales of gold in the six weeks leading up to CNY when stock-building and manufacturing are typically strong as an indication of underlying demand. We also look at trading data for the few weeks following Chinese New Year to monitor restocking by the industry which indicates whether their expectations for consumer sales were met. 

Further, we recently visited China to find more information on demand from the jewellery and investment sectors. Overall, our research indicates very strong gold jewellery demand over the Chinese New Year period and Valentine’s Day, continuing the strong buying seen throughout last year. There were, though, some signs that retailers and wholesalers may have overestimated demand a little, with restocking a little slower than had been expected. With gold prices having weakened since then, we expect further stock-building to have taken place. 

The easing of credit has also had a positive impact on gold demand. Jewellery manufacturers, retailers and other organisations have found credit a little easier to find in recent weeks and months. They have been able to build stocks but there has also been a substantial amount of collateralised buying and other uses of gold as a financial asset, leading to continued strong gold demand.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 March 2012** 

## **<mark>Silver</mark>** 

Silver prices recovered some of their old vigour in February, climbing to a new high for the year of over $37, having started the year at only $27.85. In percentage terms, this made silver a star performer although other assets such as Apple shares performed better. January’s price movement was almost a simple straight line upwards from this opening level to a closing $33.55 as the US Dollar weakened against the Euro. As the Dollar slowed its fall, silver moved sideways in a very tight range between $33 and $34.50 for the first half of February. Investors were, though, aware of what had happened in April 2011 and were building more bullish positions in advance of another assault on $40 and perhaps even $50. It was therefore somewhat odd to see a reduction in the margins applied to silver positions on COMEX on the 13<sup>th</sup> of February. This allowed investors to increase their leverage further and, although the response was not immediate, the price started to move higher from a low of $32.70 on the 16<sup>th</sup> of February. 

The first spur for the move higher was a further weakening of the US Dollar on another mild outbreak of optimism over the Greek situation. However, with margins lowered, investors decided to join the party and silver soared to a high for the year so far of $35.45 on the 23<sup>rd</sup> before stabilising and then pushing higher again on the 28<sup>th</sup> , climbing from that l

evel to $37 and even $37.40 per ounce on the 29<sup>th</sup> before gold crashed lower. Silver decided to remind investors that prices could fall as well as rise and lurched down to $34.60 at the end of the month. The price has weakened since then and silver was trading close to $32 in mid-March. 

**_Figure 6_** _: The recovery in the silver price appears impressive from close up but less so in the context of last year’s price movements. The longer tem trend appears to be lower._ 



Over the longer term, since the start of the year, silver has been held back by gold’s relative price weakness although the gold:silver ratio has moved substantially in silver’s favour, falling from 55:1 to 52:1. However, silver’s own price action is more worrying with recent highs lower each time and the low prices lower too. The price is moving in a clear downwards trend and we feel that relatively weak industrial demand will not provide much support above $25, so investor sentiment will be key. Our expectation is for lower prices in the near term although the more optimistic investor will spot a bull flag pattern which could indicate a lingering desire among investors for a move to higher prices. 

### **Physical demand for silver** 

Our recent visit to Japan gave us an opportunity to speak to producers and industrial users of silver. As we have commented previously, demand is significantly weaker than it was at the start of last year. Weakening demand for photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation systems in Europe has led to a slowdown in that industry which has been exacerbated by last year’s overstocking. Although business is improving in this industry it is doing so relatively slowly and is providing little support for prices currently. We believe

the prospects for PV demand in the second half of the year are more positive and that prices in H2 2012 have a reasonable chance of outperforming silver prices in H1. Other electronic demand remains weak however, for instance in the plasma display panel sector, although price sensitivity is relatively low at the moment. 

### **Investment demand for silver** 

Silver ETF flows have been rather anaemic so far in 2012. At the start of March, they stood at 461 million ounces, only 7 million ounces above where they were at the start of the year. In fact, this total has changed little since May 2011 when they fell back from over 500 million ounces. In part, this comparative lack of buying interest should not be too surprising given that silver has not threatened to return to anywhere close to $50 an ounce since that point However, as products like the Sprott fund prove, there is still untapped buying interest among investors. 

**_Figure 7_** _: Silver ETF flows provide little indication of investor appetite for this metal._ 



Physical investment appears to be stronger than ETF demand from our recent meetings with general c

onsumers now much more aware of the value of silver and correspondingly interested in buying silver as an investment. Unfortunately, data from the US Mint reveals that February 2012 sales of silver American Eagle coins were only 1.5 million ounces, less than half the figure sold in February 2011. Nonetheless, with January shipments having been strong we are not concerned that silver coin demand is weakening. 

**_Figure 8_** _: Like gold COMEX flows, silver COMEX flows remain a little unconvincing. However, they have recently been much more positive._

While silver ETF investors seemed rather uninterested in adding to their positions, futures investors did not share their view of the world. Net long speculative positioning on COMEX soared from 103 million ounces at the start of 2012 to 257 million ounces on the 28<sup>th</sup> of February, passing through 161 million ounces at the end of January, aided by a reduction in margins. The strong price performance was therefore no surprise. The 50 million ounce reduction in positions in early March following the price decline on the 29<sup>th</sup> of February illustrated the fragile nature of these price gains, however. Positioning last year reached a maximum of 308 million ounces, so silver could yet gain further ground. However, Chinese futures investors have not yet returned en masse and a challenge to last year’s near-record nominal prices does not seem to be imminent.

**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** 

**19 March 2012** 

## **<mark>Platinum</mark>** 

The time will come when platinum prices are once again discussed without reference to gold. However, that time has not yet arrived. We find it impossible and illogical to report on platinum’s remarkably strong price rise in the first two months of 2012 without looking at the gold price as a significant factor. At the start of the year, platinum was trading just a short distance above $1,400 after a weak end to the previous twelve months. In late February, it was trading above $1,700. In between these points, the outlook for the US economy improved somewhat and some of the issues faced by the primary platinum group metal producers came to the fore very visibly. And yet, neither price extreme really represented the reality of the supply-demand situation. 

**_Figure 9_** _: The multi-month bull run of the platinum price has come under some threat in the first half of March…._ 



While platinum was certainly oversold when it was dumped down to its lows in late 2011, it is tempting to associate the following price recovery with either an attempt to catch up with the higher gold price or with support from supply disruption or the cost of production within South Africa. In fact, all of these factors seemed to play a role, helping platinum move from an initial $1,589 at the start of February to $1,720 on the 28th of t

he month. The price action on the 29th was interesting as gold plummeted $100 in a day on Dollar strength and the belief that the prospects of a further round of quantitative easing were receding. Platinum, by contrast, fell only $65. There is little doubt that, rightly or wrongly, investors had become increasingly bullish for the platinum price and that it would eventually recapture its premium over gold, something that happened in the first half of March. 13 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **19 March 2012** ### **Platinum production** The Impala lease area strike finally ended in early March after more than a month of considerable disruption. According to the company, the strike has lead to a loss of 120,000 ounces of platinum production (and the loss of a smaller but still considerable amount of palladium output). This figure could, though, be a maximum as there may be opportunities to catch up with _some_ of the lost production later in the year. Since the end of this strike, other industrial action has broken out at another South African mine (which we will discuss more in our next monthly report). Overall, there is a reasonable chance that these disruptions could move the platinum market into deficit this year, both directly by removing some platinum supply from the market and indirectly by encouraging further physical ETF investment to add to demand. The more important issue is, though, a general worsening of the industrial relations climate. While strikes over issues such as salaries and working conditions are not particularly surprising, the greater degree of unpredictability of recent strike action is of great concern to the industry and can only be a driver for higher metal prices. Also in South Africa, the ruling party, the ANC, has decided against pursuing a process of mine nationalisation for the moment at least. Instead, the ANC has proposed imposing a new super-tax on mining, more in line with the behaviour of other commodity-rich countries. While this tax would have little impact on the platinum mining sector in terms of its competitiveness with other national mining regimes (due to the dominance of South Africa in the platinum sector), it would simply add further to costs, either squeezing operating margins or adding to upwards price pressures. Wide-ranging discussions continue between the Zimbabwean Government and the mining houses operating there too. They mainly focus on the indigenisation (nationalisation) process and it appears that some progress has been made over the Zimplats operation but not over the Mimosa mine. We would, however, caution that th

ese negotiations have not progressed in a linear fashion and it may be too early to assume that any solution has yet been reached. Additionally, concerns remain over high license fees that the Zimbabwean Government is asking mines to pay. Unless these proposed fees are reduced, there is once again a threat to the profitability and sustainability of much of Zimbabwe’s current mining operations. Meanwhile, one source of support for higher platinum prices has been removed. With the Impala strike taking place, little talk has been heard of electricity supply issues. We note that in recent weeks a number of power-hungry ferrochrome smelters have been taken offline as Eskom has “bought back” power. This demand side power management should release some of the tension from the electricity market and make load-shedding or power cuts less likely, cutting one source of support from the platinum price. ### **Platinum jewellery demand** As we have previously commented, the fact that the platinum price is below the price of gold does not automatically make platinum jewellery cheaper at a retail level than gold. However, the gap in price at Chinese retailers between the two metals has decreased to an extent and there are some signs of growing demand for platinum in this key market as a result. As with gold, we look at sales of platinum on the Shanghai Gold Exchange to give an indication of the health of jewellery demand (not all of the metal bought on the SGE is for jewellery and not all metal bought by the jewellery industry comes from SGE but trading volumes do provide some useful information). In the six weeks leading up to Chinese New Year, purchasing of platinum was stronger than in 2011 at roughly 3.5 tonnes of metal in total. This fits with our expectations of an acceptable but not outrageous increase in platinum demand. Despite some weakness at the start of March, $700 still seems to be the magic figure for this metal. **_Figure 14_** _: The palladium price seems to be steadily recovering the ground lost last year. Further challenges should lie ahead closer to $750 and $800 as and when palladium approaches those levels._ At the start of February, palladium was already moving higher from an initial $685 to a high of $716 on the 9th before weakening under pressure from a strengthening US Dollar to $678 on the 16th . When the Euro stabilised amidst continuing discussions over Greek haircuts, Greek bailouts and Greek defaults, palladium star

ted to strengthen once again, rising sharply to $698 later that day before finding $700 too hard to reach. 

The bullish move continued on the 21<sup>st</sup> when palladium soared through $700 on its way to a high of $724 on the 22<sup>nd</sup> , assisted by South African supply disruption. This move prompted some profit taking, sending palladium down to $703 on the 28<sup>th</sup> where it found support. Good US economic data provided further encouragement for many risk assets and palladium bounced to its monthly high of $724 again on the 28<sup>th</sup> . On the final day of the month, the ECB revealed how much money had been borrowed from its LTRO facility to no market reaction whatsoever. Later in the day some more anodyne comments from Ben Bernanke proved the spur for a move to a sharply stronger US Dollar. The perception that QE3 was now becoming even more unlikely to occur, took much of the energy from the commodity market and sent gold $100 higher. Palladium could not avoid some collateral damage but was fairly robust, ending the month at $702, above the support at $700. 

With palladium unable to break convincingly higher despite good ETF buying interest and supply side disruption, there must be some concern that the next major movement could be lower despite investors’ greater acceptance of risk in recent weeks. Interestingly, although we are much more positive for palladium demand than for platinum, the platinum:palladium ratio has moved fairly solidly in platinum’s favour since the start of the year, suggesting that palladium is not finding as much favour with investors. 

Viewed over a multi-month timescale, this gentle pace of price increases seems to fit well with the steady recovery from the lows of early October 2011. Since that time, the palladium price has risen by roughly a quarter, a return not to be sniffed at. However, while the price remains below $800 and the highs of last year, many investors will remain uninterested, assuming that palladium’s performance is too weak to worry about. 

Overall, therefore, we remain rather positive for the palladium price and see little reason to adjust our forecast for an average price of $745 for the year as a whole. Many of the

### **Palladium investment activity** 

Although the palladium price was unable to escape too far from $700 during February, ETF investors made their views very clear: they remain extremely bul

lish for palladium. At the start of the year, positions stood at 1.74 million ounces. At the start of March, they had reached 1.93 million ounces, taking 190,000 ounces from the market in a quarter when primary mine production would typically be lower than later in the year in any case. While prices responded slightly positively to this buying, lease rates were unchanged, suggesting that liquidity is not an issue at all. 

As we reported in our last monthly report (January), fourteen of the last sixteen weeks of 2011 saw investors disposing of more palladium from ETF holdings than they bought to add to them. During this period, average net weekly sales were 24,500 ounces of palladium. By way of comparison, Anglo Platinum itself typically produces just under 30,000 ounces of palladium per week (e.g. in Q3 2011) demonstrating just how much metal this is in market terms and exactly why the price may have fallen. 

Since the start of the new year, nine of the ten last weeks have instead seen net buying of palladium by ETF investors with average net weekly inflows of 21,200 ounces of palladium. Taken altogether, this is a swing of 45,000 ounces of additional net demand (or lower supply depending on your view of ETFs) per week. In the context of an eight million ounce-sized market, this is a very substantial change and should alone be enough to see the price strengthen. 

**_Figure 15_** _: High inflows of palladium into ETFs have provided support for the price but been unable to drive it far above $700 so far._ 



The question is why investors have changed their behaviour. We firmly believe that ETF investors tend to follow prices as well as influence them. Interestingly, the buying interest came primarily from North American investors, a sharp reversal of the picture in the second half of 2011. With palladium significantly higher than its late 2011 lows, there is plenty of positive sentiment around in the market and we expect continued buying to be seen. If prices remain close to $700 for a more extended period, buying interest could decrease.
